newsitem.title: USA: Bears are out of hibernation; roaming Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Bears are out of hibernation; roaming Wall Street.

text.p: It's spring time and the bears are out of hibernation and this comes as bad news for the stock market.
Investors rushed for the exits this week as they feared that rising interest rates would erode corporate earnings.

The Dow Jones industrial average was sent into a tailspin, with waves of selling wiping out all of the blue-chip's gain for the year, disappointing investors who poured billions of dollars into stock mutual funds over the last couple of years.
In afternoon trading Friday, the world's most closely-watched stock index was off 44.56 points at 6,432.79, which was below its 1997 start of 6,448.27. For the week, it was off a solid 307.80 points.
Less than a month ago, the Dow was tearing into record ground, leaping to 7,085.16 on a perfect investment climate.
The market's pullback was the worst since a 10 percent slump in February 1994 when the Federal Reserve started to furiously raise interest rates, a monetary tightening that ended in February 1995.

The latest shakeout was a hot topic of conversations from Wall Street to Main Street. For the first time in more than six years, the bull market was heading in reverse, leaving behind some nasty bear tracks.

Some experts said they were bracing for more erosion, as investors, who have been buying stocks for various reasons over the years, now find themselves selling for just one reason -- fear of higher interest rates.
A 10 percent drop is viewed as just simply a correction, while a 20 percent plunge is a more serious bear market, one that could last anywhere from six months to a year or more.
But many traders were not waiting to find out how low is low. They shifted out of stocks and put their money in bonds, which are currently seen as an attractive a safe haven.

"We're in a bear market, the first since 1990 and our downside objective for the Dow is 6,200 with the possibility that it could go as low as 5,800 between now and October," said Don Hays, director of investment strategy for Wheat First Butcher Singer in Richmond, Va.
Hays, a long-time bull, said Wall Street is witnessing the end of one of history's most spectacular markets, which has thrived on disinflation and low interest rates.
The downward spiral was ignited by the Fed's decision a week earlier to raise short-term interest rates by a quarter-percentage-point.

The central bank's move, the first increase in more than two years in an effort to head off inflation and slow the economy's growth, set off a chain reaction that raised borrowing costs for consumers and corporations, from credit cards to mortgages.
The threat of more interest-rate hikes will hound the market for months.

On Friday, the government reported more evidence that the economy was still in a fast track. The jobless rate fell to 5.2 percent last month from 5.3 percent and hourly wages rose, fuelling speculation that central bankers will raise rates again, possibly as soon as their next meeting on May 20.
Hays said investors will have to lower their expectations of stocks now that one of the pillars of the bull market -- stable interest rates -- has been removed.

For the next several years, he said, the annual appreciation for the Dow and other large-capitalisation indexes will slow to an average 6 percent, a fraction of the returns of the last two years. In 1996, the Dow jumped 26 percent after racking up a 33.5 percent gain in 1995.
Hays said the market was undergoing the first of many phases of the decline, and he expected stocks to find some temporary support on the way down.
"It will have a little sabbatical before coming down once again later but for now, it's so oversold that it will have to do some healing."
Hays said stocks became over-valued four weeks ago, when most of his firm's investment models turned negative, signalling that the bull market had lost its footing.
"Only market psychology stayed strong, but it's impossible to move a market just on psychology," he said.
The market's rout sobered a lot of overly optimistic investors who believed that stocks could only go up.

The market's inability to rally suggested that many investors were not in a rush to buy back, sensing that the bearish mentality was still in control of the market and stocks could be cheaper down the road.

Mutual fund investors also were pulling in their horns, as the flows into U.S. stock mutual funds shrank to $46 million for the two-day period ended March 31 from $1.29 billion for the three trading days ended March 26, according to Mutual Fund Trim Tabs.

A shortage of mutual fund cash to drive stocks higher could further damage the market because the longer the buyers stay on the sidelines, the tougher it will be for new sellers to find buyers, which would lead to even lower prices.
Also likely to keep some investors awake at night is the risk of a market meltdown if mutual fund investors and momentum traders race against one another to liquidate their holdings.
Momentum traders buy stocks in anticipation of strong corporate growth but are quick to sell on hints of bad news.

"We are seeing the unwinding of momentum investing, which is not made up of long-term traders who buy shares in companies because of long term fundamentals but instead, they are treating the market as a gambling arena," said Steve Halpern, publisher of the Dick Davis Digest, an investment newsletter in Fort Lauderdale, Fla.

"People have been buying stocks just simply because stocks have been going up and they think that someone will pay a higher price," he said. "Those people who were playing the market for the wrong reasons are all going to be swept out before this market correction is over."
Halpern expects the Dow to fall 1,000 points from its record high in March before the dust settles.
